region: Southeastern Australia and Tasmania; planted elsewhere
description: Australian blackwood is a medium-density acacia with golden to dark reddish-brown heartwood, often with striking curly or fiddleback figure. It is used for fine furniture, cabinetry, veneer, and musical instruments such as guitars and ukuleles.

hazards.summary: Occupational asthma from blackwood dust was reported in Australian woodworkers, and a NIOSH-funded review lists it among woods with a positive specific challenge test.

Blackwood has long been reported to cause allergic skin rashes in Australian woodworkers. Lab studies identified several heartwood compounds that can sensitize skin, though their individual strength appears modest.
All wood dust, including Australian blackwood, is classified by IARC as carcinogenic to humans, mainly linked to cancers of the nose and sinuses after long-term exposure.

related_species_note: Hausen-1990 notes melacacidin occurs in many other Acacia species, so related acacia woods could plausibly cause similar skin reactions; this has not been confirmed species by species.

notes_internal: WoodBaker-1997 and Clarke-1989 have no abstracts; level 1 rests on SENSOR-2017 Table 3 listing (positive specific challenge). Skin evidence kept at level 3: Hausen papers are guinea-pig sensitisation and chemistry; Tilsley-1990 (clinical report, no abstract) may include human patch tests - if so upgrade to level 1. Hausen-1981 abstract also mentions 'toxic effects' since 1925 without detail - not entered. Name checked on GBIF only. No reports for a given effect does not mean the wood is safe.
